newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK MUTUAL FUNDS WARY OF BOND INCOME TAX IMPACT.
newsitem.headline: GREEK MUTUAL FUNDS WARY OF BOND INCOME TAX IMPACT.

text.p: The imposition of a 15 percent tax on income from coupon stripping and bond trading by Greek mutual funds as per a finance ministry memorandum threatens the bond market and the mutual fund industry, market players said.

The recent finance ministry memorandum aims to clarify tax issues related to law 2275/94 and legal experts say it would be applied retroactively unless the finance ministry sets a new date for tax calculation purposes.

"The memorandum creates enormous problems to the financing of the budget deficit, the secondary bond market, the money market and fixed income mutual funds and their shareholders," said a fund manager at a foreign mutual fund company.

Faced with a huge public debt that exceeds 110 percent of GDP and large annual debt servicing payments burdening the budget deficit, the treasury has engaged in more active debt management to extend the average maturity of the public debt.
The treasury's decision to adopt frequent auctions for floaters, mainly seven-year FRNs, works in that direction and institutionals are among their best fans.

The traditional issues of 12-month, six-month and three-month T-bills with administratively set rates continue and retail investors seem to be fond of them but T-bills have lost some of their previous luster with funds.

Adverse effects on secondary bond trading can already be detected as mutual funds and investment companies are trying to figure out the implications of the tax and find out how the finance ministry will react to these developments, bankers said.
Mutual funds and investment companies are major players in the primary and secondary bond markets along with commercial banks.

"The finance ministry is pre-occupied with raising tax revenues to slash the deficit and fails to realise that it will pay much more in interest payments on its debt by driving institutionals out of the primary and secondary bond market," said a fund manager at a private mutual fund management company.

Press reports have finance ministry officials outraged by sales of stripped coupons to retail investors by banks and institutionals, offering slightly better yields than T-bills around the same time T-bill issues come out.
The finance ministry does not tax individual buyers of state securities such as T-bills and FRNs but taxes the interest income institutions earn from them.
This differential tax treatment accounts for many market distortions and has institutional investors on the look out for investment vehicles that will by-pass the tax.
Bankers, mutual fund managers and other market watchers were quick to point out problems relating to who would shoulder the tax burden if the tax law went into effect retroactively.

"Making current shareholders bear the whole tax burden would be unfair and reduce their returns substantially," said a fund manager at a foreign mutual fund. "But sharing the tax burden equally would be almost impossible since old shareholders have redeemed their mutual fund shares."

It is not clear what will be the exact impact on current mutual fund shareholders but industry officials said holders of fixed income fund shares would be hit harder than shareholders of money market funds.

Although allocations vary within the same class of mutual funds, money market funds hold on average about 20 to 50 percent of their assets in bonds with fixed income fund allocations ranging from 60 to 90 percent.

And based on published first-half results, a money market fund of a private bank has almost 90 percent of its assets in bonds. This does not square well with capital market commission guidelines, fund managers say.
Other market watchers put the blame squarely on mutual fund management companies which failed to make tax provisions although they knew that the imprecision of the particular law warranted caution.

"It is not the first time that public sector officials write a tax law without fully understanding its implications and move to clarify it much later," said an executive at a foreign bank. "The mutual fund industry should have known it and taken precautionary measures."
Mutual funds that have made provisions for the tax can be counted in the fingers of one hand, said an informed industry source.

"Who is going to bail out the funds if the finance ministry sticks to the law and asks for the payment of penalties and back taxes," he asked. "Many AEDAKs (mutual fund management companies) might not be able to do it and in some cases it could be the parent banks."
"But what will be the effect on the bank's results if it did so?, he asked.
-- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
